questions.stem: Improve the underlined part: She is one of the students who _____ topped the exam.
questions.explanation: 'One of the + plural noun + who' takes a PLURAL verb, because 'who' refers back to 'students' (plural), not to 'one'. Hence 'have topped'. Very high-hit rule.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Improve: He is senior _____ me by two years.
questions.explanation: 'Senior/junior/superior/inferior/prior to' — ALL take 'to', never 'than'. The -or ending already implies comparison.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Improve: The child fell down ____ the stairs.
questions.explanation: 'Fell from the stairs' — indicating origin. 'Fell down' alone is fine but the 'stairs' noun needs a 'from' to complete the movement-source.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Improve: No sooner had the bell rung _____ the students rushed out.
questions.explanation: Fixed correlative pair: 'No sooner … THAN'. 'Scarcely/Hardly … when'. Examiners routinely swap these two to test the student.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Improve: The scissors _____ on the table.
questions.explanation: Scissors is a plural-only noun (pluralia tantum). Same group: trousers, spectacles, pants, tongs. Always plural verb.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Improve: Each of the boys _____ given a prize.
questions.explanation: 'Each' is the subject → singular verb 'was'. Rule: each/every/either/neither/none + singular verb, regardless of the plural noun that follows.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Improve: If I _____ you, I would accept the offer.
questions.explanation: Subjunctive mood for hypothetical / unreal conditions: 'If I WERE you' (all persons). 'If I was' is informal / wrong in formal exam English.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Improve: Hardly had he entered the room _____ the lights went out.
questions.explanation: Pair: 'Hardly / Scarcely … WHEN'. Different from 'No sooner … THAN'. Memorise the two pairs together; they're the Banking / SSC bread-and-butter.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Improve: The quality of these mangoes _____ poor.
questions.explanation: Subject is 'quality' (singular); 'of these mangoes' is a prepositional phrase that does NOT change the subject. Verb must match the head noun.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Improve: She has been ill _____ Monday.
questions.explanation: Rule: SINCE + point in time (Monday, 2019, 9 a.m.). FOR + duration (two days, three hours). Both require present perfect. 'From' is wrong in this perfect-tense frame.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The underlined part of the following sentence may need improvement. Choose the best alternative: 'She was married **with** a renowned cardiologist and moved to Mumbai.'
questions.explanation: The correct preposition after 'married' is 'to', not 'with'. We always say 'married to someone'. Option A ('by') is a passive-voice agent marker, not a relational preposition. Option C ('for') implies purpose, not union — it is ungrammatical in this context.

questions.stem: Select the option that best improves the underlined part: 'Despite **of** his sincere preparation, he could not crack the interview.'
questions.explanation: 'Despite' is a preposition that is directly followed by a noun or noun phrase — never by 'of'. The error arises from confusion with 'in spite of', which does take 'of'. Options A and B introduce further incorrect prepositions ('with', 'for') that are grammatically invalid after 'despite'.

questions.stem: Choose the best replacement for the underlined part: 'The manager suggested **to postpone the meeting** until further notice.'

options.option_text: to have postponed the meeting early

questions.explanation: After verbs like 'suggest', 'recommend', 'consider', and 'avoid', a gerund (-ing form) must be used, not a to-infinitive. 'Suggested to postpone' is a common SSC/banking error; 'suggested postponing' is the correct construction. Option A introduces 'for', which wrongly turns the construction into a prepositional phrase.

questions.stem: Identify the error and select the improvement: 'Being a cold winter morning, **the heater was switched on by Meera immediately**.'

options.option_text: Meera immediately switched on the heater
the heater had been switched on quickly
the heater was immediately switched on
No improvement is required here at all

questions.explanation: This is a dangling modifier error. The participial phrase 'Being a cold winter morning' must logically modify the subject of the main clause. Since Meera is the one experiencing the cold morning, she must be the grammatical subject: 'Meera immediately switched on the heater'. Options B and C both retain a passive construction, which leaves the participial phrase without a logical referent.

questions.stem: Choose the option that corrects the underlined part: 'The course requires students to attend lectures, **completing assignments**, and take examinations.'
questions.explanation: The three items listed after 'requires students to' must be parallel infinitives: 'to attend', 'to complete (assignments)', and 'to take'. 'Completing' (a gerund) breaks the parallel structure. Option C restores parallelism as a bare infinitive matching 'attend' and 'take'. Option A introduces 'for', which disrupts the infinitive chain entirely.

questions.stem: Select the best improvement for the underlined part: 'He ran as fast as he could lest he **may** miss the last train to Howrah.'

options.option_text: might miss the last train to Howrah
should miss the last train to Howrah
would miss the last train to Howrah
could miss the last train to Howrah

questions.explanation: After 'lest', the auxiliary 'should' is obligatory in formal English: the structure is 'lest + subject + should + V1'. Neither 'may' nor 'might' is used after 'lest'. Option A ('might') is the strongest distractor because it expresses possibility, which is semantically close — but grammatically, 'lest' categorically demands 'should'. 'Would' and 'could' convey volition and ability respectively, neither of which fits the fearful purpose expressed by 'lest'.

questions.stem: Identify the error and choose the correct improvement: '**A number of students in the class was** absent due to the harvest festival.'

options.option_text: A number of students in the class were
The number of students in the class was
A number of students in the class are
No improvement is required here at all

questions.explanation: 'A number of' means 'several/many' and always governs a plural verb: 'A number of students were absent'. The sentence wrongly uses the singular 'was'. Option B ('The number of students was') is grammatically correct but changes the meaning entirely — 'the number' refers to a counted quantity and takes a singular verb. This contrast (a number of = plural; the number of = singular) is one of the highest-frequency subject-verb traps in SSC CGL and IBPS PO papers. Option C uses 'are', which is wrong tense for a completed past event.
